title: Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018
short_title: Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would allow a person removed from Australia who is returned because the removal was aborted or the receiving country refused entry to re-enter lawfully without a visa.
It would let the Department of Home Affairs use online accounts like ImmiAccount to send legally required communications to clients.
The bill would also add a new power to make regulations setting fees for paying or recovering the passenger movement charge.
changes: Amends the Migration Act to provide a lawful basis for return without a visa for certain unsuccessful removals.
Amends the Customs Act to allow the department to make recoverable payments to entitled persons.
Amends the Passenger Movement Charge Collection Act to allow regulations for charging and recovering fees related to the passenger movement charge.
summary.affected: Unlawful non-citizens subject to removal, the Department of Home Affairs, persons entitled to recoverable payments, and entities paying or dealing with the passenger movement charge.

divisions.stage: Returned from the House of Representatives

speeches.speaker: Alex Hawke
speeches.brief: The Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018 amends the Migration Act to allow return of unlawful noncitizens without a visa in more circumstances, such as transit refusal or UN Human Rights Committee interim measures, and clarifies that visa application bars continue as if they never left. It also enables document delivery via online accounts, inserts a power to refund duty when overpaid, recovers merchant fees for credit card payments, and makes minor technical amendments to the Customs Act.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: The speech supported the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018 while accusing the Minister for Home Affairs of mismanagement. It cited partner visa processing times rising from 19 to 30 months for 90% of applications, more than 176,000 bridging visas, and an ANAO report finding only two of 33 consultant contracts were evaluated.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: The Greens argued the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018 contains provisions that bar asylum seekers returned to Australia after a third country refuses them from reapplying for protection, which the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights flagged as a human rights concern. The Greens will further examine the bill in the Senate and do not support it.

speeches.speaker: Alex Hawke
speeches.brief: The Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018 amends the Migration Act 1958, Customs Act 1901, and Passenger Movement Charge Collection Act 1978. Key changes include allowing unlawful noncitizens returned to Australia after a failed removal to re-enter without a visa, permitting the Department of Home Affairs to use ImmiAccount for legal communications, enabling recoverable customs payments, controlling movement between sea installations and the coast, regulating disposal of narcotic-related goods, and prescribing fees for passenger movement charge collection.

speeches.speaker: Christian Porter
speeches.brief: The government moved to reject Senate amendments to the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment Bill, arguing they would unconstitutionally increase public expenditure from standing appropriations by requiring the minister to appoint at least six doctors to a health panel. The speaker claimed Labor had supported the amendments in December 2018 without security agency advice, then withdrew support months later, and warned that accepting the amendments would breach 109 years of House of Representatives practice and section 53 of the Constitution by allowing the Senate to initiate spending.

speeches.speaker: Tony Burke
speeches.brief: The speaker moved an amendment to set aside constitutional disputes with the Senate over the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018, citing public interest in speedy passage, and noted that the Howard government had moved an identical resolution in November 1996.
